Stated Claim / Post Context:
Police investigate report of sexual assault at a fraternity party near the University of Chicago

Police are investigating a report that a woman was sexually assaulted during a fraternity party near the University of Chicago campus.

Actual Article Body:
CHICAGO (AP) — Police are investigating a woman’s report that she was sexually assaulted during a fraternity party near the University of Chicago campus, an allegation that comes at a time of heightened awareness of sexual violence on college campuses.

Chicago police said no one had been charged Wednesday, a day after university officials posted an alert saying that a person of interest had been identified.

The Chicago case comes amid an uproar over Cornell University’s handling of a woman’s allegations that she was drugged and gang raped by fraternity members in 2024. A campus investigation led to internal disciplinary action by the university, but no criminal charges were ever filed.

The University of Chicago, a top-ranked U.S. research school with an enrollment of 18,000 students, said in a statement that a woman reported being sexually assaulted early Sunday during a party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house.

The university said the perpetrator fled the house after being confronted by another person.

The 21-year-old woman reported the assault to police and went to a hospital for treatment, according to Chicago police. The university said she is not a student.

Chicago police did not immediately provide a copy of the incident report on the alleged attack when The Associated Press requested it Wednesday.

The Chicago Sun-Times, citing the police report, said the woman told police she had been drinking and dancing at the party before she began feeling unwell. The Sun-Times said the report stated two of the woman’s friends then found her “not fully conscious” in a bathroom with a man and that both were partially undressed.

The friends told police that to get into the bathroom, they had to force their way through several men who were “cheering and appearing to encourage the activity inside,” the Sun-Times reported.

Alpha Epsilon Pi said no fraternity members took part in the alleged attack or encouraged it. The fraternity’s University of Chicago chapter said in a statement that its members rushed to help the woman after being alerted by one of her friends and ended the party immediately.

“There is no evidence at all that any AEPi members participated in this assault or were aware of it while it was transpiring,” Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity’s national organization, said in a statement Wednesday.

The fraternity said the perpetrator was chased out of the house and was recorded by cameras while fleeing.

University officials said the person of interest who has been identified is not a student or otherwise affiliated with the school.

The Cornell case came to light last month after a woman filed a lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members, saying she was repeatedly assaulted at a fraternity house in October 2024. She went to campus police three weeks later and gave a detailed interview, but local prosecutors never pursued charges. The men she accused have denied wrongdoing.

Cornell announced Tuesday it’s banning parties at fraternity houses until next year. The university said it will include New York State Police in investigations of campus sexual assaults.

Fraternities have also been under scrutiny at the University of Arizona, which suspended fraternity activities earlier this month following multiple reports of assault, hazing and other misconduct.

___

Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.

A hundred worshippers at Holy Name Cathedral bowed their heads to pray for the recovery of Chicago native Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday after the pontiff’s lung cancer diagnosis just hours prior. 
“We humbly entreat you, Lord … as you have entrusted Leo with the office of shepherd, grant him always salvation and protection, together with the flock entrusted to his care,” said the Rev. Louis Cameli during Mass, which was dedicated to the health and healing of the Holy Father. 
Across the Chicago area, Catholic faithful have been praying for their hometown pontiff’s convalescence after the lower section of his right lung was removed Tuesday and physicians diagnosed him with adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. 
“We need him more than ever in this moment we are living,” said Carmen Daley, 72, who attended the Mass at Holy Name. “We are praying for his health, that God will take care of him and for a speedy recovery.” 
Cameli noted the Holy Father “is not only for us Catholics, but he has emerged as a very important voice for the whole world.” 
Friends of the pope took heart Wednesday after doctors reported that Leo was up and walking again, resuming his regular diet and undergoing respiratory exercises, as he healed from Tuesday’s procedure. 
A chest X-ray and blood tests indicated the 71-year-old pope was recovering normally, according to two physicians. 
“Everyone is concerned. But most people follow the hopeful prognosis that the doctors gave,” said the Rev. John Lydon, the pope’s longtime friend and former roommate when they were missionaries together in Peru during the 1990s. “I have been praying a lot for him and a quick recovery.” 				
					
				
Lydon was in Rome for an international sustainability conference that Leo had also been scheduled to attend before his surgery. 
The priest was surprised by the lung cancer diagnosis, noting when the Holy Father had mentioned his upcoming surgery during remarks on Sunday, “it was kind of a low-key announcement.” 
“So we just thought it might be something simple,” said Lydon, who around this time last year had met with Leo in his Vatican apartment and rode alongside him in the popemobile. “It didn’t turn out to be as simple as we had hoped it would be.”

Lydon said he and the other conference attendees learned of the diagnosis late Tuesday. 				
					
				
“Because he’s a friend, I’m very concerned and sad,” said Lydon, who served at the Augustinian house in Hyde Park until May, when he transferred to Villanova University, his and Leo’s alma mater. “When it’s someone you personally know… it hits you differently. So in that sense, I felt very saddened by the news — but balancing it with the hopefulness that the doctors have manifested.” 
People pray during the noon Mass with special prayers for Pope Leo XIV at Holy Name Cathedral on Oct. 14, 2026. (Antonio Perez/Chicago Tribune)
Although lung cancer is the most deadly form of cancer worldwide, it can be very treatable if caught early, which appears to be the case for the pope. 
Lydon noted Leo is otherwise very healthy and active; his friend and fellow Augustinian is known to be an avid tennis player and frequent exerciser as well. 
Cardinal Blase Cupich asked that “people of good will everywhere, but particularly here, in Pope Leo’s hometown, join me in asking the Lord to return this son of Chicago to wellness.” 
“While this is not the news we hoped for, we are heartened by the skill and optimism of his physicians and the countless prayers offered around the world for his complete recovery,” the archbishop of Chicago said in a statement. “He has much more good work to do, many more wise words to preach and many more ways to inspire others.” 
The Chicago area burst in celebration after Leo’s groundbreaking May 2025 selection as pope, marking the first American pontiff in church history.

Dozens of people from the Chicago area have since met with the Holy Father at the Vatican, including Gov. JB Pritzker, Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson and a group of students from Our Lady of Mount Carmel Academy in the Lakeview neighborhood who went viral last year for hosting a mock papal conclave. 
The students gathered Wednesday morning to pray for Pope Leo and sent him a care package that included handmade get-well cards and a White Sox blanket, a nod to the pontiff’s devotion to his hometown team.

The pope’s schedule has been cleared through Oct. 20 as he heals from surgery. 
A group of Chicago-area clergy and religious leaders who are scheduled to visit Leo on Oct. 27 to advocate on behalf of immigrant detainees say they haven’t heard about any change of plans.

“The Vatican’s announcement of Pope Leo’s cancer diagnosis has only deepened our profound appreciation for him as the head of the global Catholic church,” the Chicago-based Coalition for Spiritual and Public Leadership said in a statement. “He has taken a stand for the dignity and worth of all people.” 
On Tuesday, a group of a half-dozen Vatican leaders in Chicago for a conference gathered at Leo’s childhood home in south suburban Dolton to pray for him as he underwent surgery. 
“We were there just giving thanks for the gift of his life and praying that God would grant him many, many more days,” said Joe Boland, chief mission officer for the Chicago-based Catholic Extension Society, which organized the pilgrimage. 
The cancer diagnosis was devastating for Boland, as if the illness was discovered in a family member or other close loved one. 
He recalled meeting with the Holy Father at the Vatican in May alongside his organization’s executive director, the Rev. Jack Wall, who also grew up in Dolton just seven blocks from the home of the pope.

The pontiff greeted them saying, “I heard someone is here from Dolton, Illinois. And when someone from Dolton, Illinois comes, we have to open all the doors,” Boland recalled.

“He’s been given a global mission…. But his heart is still connected to this city,” Boland added. “And that is a powerful thing to be from essentially the same place that the pope is from. We understand the unique nuances of the man and where he grew up and what the influences were in his life. We see how that shapes him in his global ministry. And that’s a privileged place for us as Chicagoans.”

The Associated Press contributed.

America’s top party college rocked by sorority girl scandal as California sisters go scorched earth: ‘We all noticed’

The drama began during fall recruitment in late September.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A sorority scandal has erupted at one of America’s most notorious party schools after members accused an outside recruitment adviser of sidelining women of color, sparking a furious showdown inside their California chapter house.

Sisters of the Alpha Phi sorority at the University of California, Santa Barbara, say they were left stunned when Black women and other women of color were allegedly excluded from recruitment activities while prospective members from diverse backgrounds mysteriously disappeared from the selection pool, according to the Daily Nexus.

The explosive allegations have rocked the coastal campus, with outrage spilling onto social media and sorority sisters turning against the very leadership brought in to help them recruit new members.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Never miss a story

“All of us started to notice,” chapter president Alana Nielsen told the student newspaper. “It was not just one. It was not just a few. It was not just the women of color. It was all of us.”

The drama began during fall recruitment in late September, when Alpha Phi International sent three representatives to oversee the chapter’s annual rush process.

Among them was a volunteer recruitment adviser who was also a UCSB Alpha Phi alumna and had assisted the chapter for the previous two years.

Roughly 1,200 hopefuls initially participated in recruitment, according to the Santa Barbara News-Press.

But after the first round on Sept. 26, sorority members were reportedly ordered to leave while the outside representatives determined which candidates would advance.

When the sisters returned, the pool had reportedly shrunk to approximately 250 women and members immediately noticed something troubling.

“There was a large and noticeably diverse group of women who were missing from the pool of potential new members that had returned,” Nielsen told the Daily Nexus.

The apparent shake-up was especially baffling because members had reportedly been told that roughly 90% of prospective recruits mutually wanted to return to Alpha Phi.

Meanwhile, existing sisters of color were allegedly being pushed to the sidelines.

Sky Achola, a Black sorority member and third-year political science major, said she arrived at the house Sept. 27 expecting to meet prospective recruits, only to discover she had been left off the schedule entirely.

She soon realized she wasn’t alone.

“Pretty much all the women of color in my family system, except for my ‘little,’ who was white, were pulled from all the rounds,” Achola told the News-Press.

Achola said she was eventually assigned to one recruitment round after members began raising questions.

“I actually personally was in a state of shock for about three days,” she told the outlet.

As the alleged discrimination became increasingly apparent, frustration inside the sorority house reached a boiling point.

Nielsen said she requested a chapter-wide meeting to address the concerns but was allegedly told by an outside representative that a discussion was unnecessary and that the day should end on a “happy note.”

Instead of sending the sisters home, Nielsen gathered members in the chapter room for an emotional confrontation.

What followed was nothing short of a sorority revolt.

“Girls [were] standing up screaming,” recruitment director Emerson Novosel told the Daily Nexus. “It [was] like a revolution happening right now. Like standing up, crying, screaming, and I had never felt so empowered.”

Members demanded answers as some broke down in tears, accusing the outside leadership of betraying the chapter’s values.

The volunteer adviser reportedly left the meeting after objecting to the confrontation.

Later that night, chapter recruitment directors met with the two remaining international representatives and learned that the volunteer had been responsible for deciding which prospective members advanced and which sisters participated in recruitment groups, according to chapter leaders.

The unidentified adviser was subsequently reported and removed from her position.

“It had [become] so disgustingly clear how it was just manipulation, just blatant manipulation to every part of the process with whatever her hidden agenda is,” Novosel told the Daily Nexus.

The controversy quickly exploded across Yik Yak, the anonymous social media platform popular among college students, where posts demanding accountability racked up hundreds and sometimes more than 1,000 upvotes, per the News-Press.

But the sisters insist they were victims of the alleged discrimination too.

“The women of color in the sorority were discriminated against too,” Achola told the News-Press.

Despite the uproar, Alpha Phi refused to abandon recruitment, with the national organization choosing instead to take control of the remaining process.

The chapter ultimately filled its recruitment quota, leaving uncertainty over whether women allegedly excluded earlier could still receive invitations through a separate informal bidding process.

On Oct. 1, members released a collective statement through an anonymous Instagram account, declaring they would fight for change from within.

“We have chosen to remain in the recruitment process because we believe that our members have the power to create meaningful change from within,” the statement read.

Alpha Phi International later sent representatives from its health, wellness and accountability department to meet with chapter members, including at an Oct. 5 meeting.

Nielsen said the chapter is collecting statements from members and pushing to overhaul recruitment procedures.

For Achola, the fallout has been especially painful.

“We were extremely hurt by this entire thing. We were discriminated against. We were tokenized. We were used,” she told the Daily Nexus.

And while the sorority’s reputation has taken a beating, Nielsen insisted the sisters are determined to make sure the scandal doesn’t happen again.

“That’s going to be a relationship that’s going to take a long time to repair,” she said of the chapter’s relationship with its national leadership.

The California Post reached out to Alpha Phi International and UCSB for comment.

Roughly 1,200 hopefuls initially participated in recruitment, according to the Santa Barbara News-Press.

But after the first round on Sept. 26, sorority members were reportedly ordered to leave while the outside representatives determined which candidates would advance.

When the sisters returned, the pool had reportedly shrunk to approximately 250 women and members immediately noticed something troubling.

“There was a large and noticeably diverse group of women who were missing from the pool of potential new members that had returned,” Nielsen told the Daily Nexus.

The apparent shake-up was especially baffling because members had reportedly been told that roughly 90% of prospective recruits mutually wanted to return to Alpha Phi.

Meanwhile, existing sisters of color were allegedly being pushed to the sidelines.

Sky Achola, a Black sorority member and third-year political science major, said she arrived at the house Sept. 27 expecting to meet prospective recruits, only to discover she had been left off the schedule entirely.

She soon realized she wasn’t alone.

“Pretty much all the women of color in my family system, except for my ‘little,’ who was white, were pulled from all the rounds,” Achola told the News-Press.

Achola said she was eventually assigned to one recruitment round after members began raising questions.

“I actually personally was in a state of shock for about three days,” she told the outlet.

As the alleged discrimination became increasingly apparent, frustration inside the sorority house reached a boiling point.

Nielsen said she requested a chapter-wide meeting to address the concerns but was allegedly told by an outside representative that a discussion was unnecessary and that the day should end on a “happy note.”

Instead of sending the sisters home, Nielsen gathered members in the chapter room for an emotional confrontation.

What followed was nothing short of a sorority revolt.

“Girls [were] standing up screaming,” recruitment director Emerson Novosel told the Daily Nexus. “It [was] like a revolution happening right now. Like standing up, crying, screaming, and I had never felt so empowered.”

Members demanded answers as some broke down in tears, accusing the outside leadership of betraying the chapter’s values.

The volunteer adviser reportedly left the meeting after objecting to the confrontation.

Later that night, chapter recruitment directors met with the two remaining international representatives and learned that the volunteer had been responsible for deciding which prospective members advanced and which sisters participated in recruitment groups, according to chapter leaders.

The unidentified adviser was subsequently reported and removed from her position.

“It had [become] so disgustingly clear how it was just manipulation, just blatant manipulation to every part of the process with whatever her hidden agenda is,” Novosel told the Daily Nexus.

The controversy quickly exploded across Yik Yak, the anonymous social media platform popular among college students, where posts demanding accountability racked up hundreds and sometimes more than 1,000 upvotes, per the News-Press.

But the sisters insist they were victims of the alleged discrimination too.

“The women of color in the sorority were discriminated against too,” Achola told the News-Press.

Despite the uproar, Alpha Phi refused to abandon recruitment, with the national organization choosing instead to take control of the remaining process.

The chapter ultimately filled its recruitment quota, leaving uncertainty over whether women allegedly excluded earlier could still receive invitations through a separate informal bidding process.

On Oct. 1, members released a collective statement through an anonymous Instagram account, declaring they would fight for change from within.

“We have chosen to remain in the recruitment process because we believe that our members have the power to create meaningful change from within,” the statement read.

Alpha Phi International later sent representatives from its health, wellness and accountability department to meet with chapter members, including at an Oct. 5 meeting.

Nielsen said the chapter is collecting statements from members and pushing to overhaul recruitment procedures.

For Achola, the fallout has been especially painful.

“We were extremely hurt by this entire thing. We were discriminated against. We were tokenized. We were used,” she told the Daily Nexus.

And while the sorority’s reputation has taken a beating, Nielsen insisted the sisters are determined to make sure the scandal doesn’t happen again.

“That’s going to be a relationship that’s going to take a long time to repair,” she said of the chapter’s relationship with its national leadership.

The California Post reached out to Alpha Phi International and UCSB for comment.
